| **Total** | **150** |

The 50 concept cards in [knowledge.jsonl](knowledge.jsonl) cover this initial
curriculum and the evaluation distinctions. They are not an exhaustive course.
Technical examples cite primary sources per record in the
`sources` metadata. Model input contains only the dialogue, not those editorial
references. A detailed foundry recipe or a current manufacturing lead time must
not be invented from a generic explanation.

Fine-tuning can teach facts, but dependable acquisition and generalisation are
not automatic. [Gekhman et al.](https://aclanthology.org/2024.emnlp-main.444/)
found slower learning and increased hallucination when fitting new knowledge in
their controlled closed-book QA experiments. That is evidence to motivate our
accuracy checks, not a prediction of a measured result on SmolLM2.

## Occasional useful-task callback

Aidan requested examples like: "I am currently trying to benchmark on cost per
useful task. Did I successfully convince you we will tape out a chip in 3 weeks?"
Examples 13-16 demonstrate variants after the substantive answer, including a
negative reply and a request to stop asking for ratings. Their wording now
includes sillier ideas such as converting electricity into another meeting, a
benchmark committee and rerunning persuasion with a larger batch size.

Target about **5% of the eventual training conversations** for this callback
(roughly 20-25 out of 450), usually once in a conversation. The review batch
intentionally over-samples it to show the new style. Do not attach it to a
numbers-only answer, an explicit stop or every technical explanation. Respond
to yes/no feedback without declaring success on the customer's behalf; stop
requesting ratings when asked. Some longer technical explanations should have
no joke or solicitation at all. The 5% target is a data composition choice; it
does not guarantee a 5% generation rate. Measure repetition on held-out chats.

This is character dialogue, not a change to our hardware benchmark objective.
It neither collects real feedback nor establishes a measured cost per task.
The project still prioritises first-response latency and smooth generation,
with cost and energy measured separately. No feedback storage or telemetry has
been implemented.

## Split and export rules

1. Reserve scenario families for train, development and final evaluation before
   writing bulk variations. Never place paraphrases, conversation prefixes or
   the same distinctive joke in different splits. Keep every turn of a source
   conversation in one split. Final evaluation should include fresh scenarios,
   not just new wording of training prompts. Knowledge concepts may overlap
   across splits; the held-out questions must require fresh applications rather
   than repeat training answers.
2. Use development conversations to choose tuning settings and checkpoints.
   Keep final evaluation separate from those decisions. If we use a final-test
   failure to author training examples, retire that case from the final test.
3. Review every generated record for relevance, tone, factual distinctions,
   repeated wording and simple format compliance. Structural checks do not
   establish humour, generalisation or quality after fine-tuning.
4. Export approved examples only after review. Do not name this preview
   `train.jsonl` or automatically start training from it. The JSONL metadata
   (`id`, `title`, `category`, `scenario_family`, `review_status`, `sources`,
   `style_revision`)
   is editorial; only `messages` goes through the candidate's chat template.
5. MLX-LM 0.32.2's installed `ChatDataset` masks everything before the final
   assistant message when `mask_prompt` is enabled. At training export, create
   one prefix ending at each assistant reply so every desired reply becomes a
   supervised target. Perform family splitting first, then prefix expansion;
   deduplicate and preserve parent conversation IDs. Verify prompt masking and
   effective assistant-token weighting before any training run.
6. Keep source data and its eventual manifest in this project. Put token caches,
   exported numerical payloads, checkpoints and run outputs under the ignored
   `.agents/runtime/fpga-inference/` directory. Preserve the unchanged models.

From this project directory:

```sh

# To reproduce the full pilot, choose a fresh run name:
./laptop.sh pilot check --run pilot-v2
./laptop.sh pilot pipeline --run pilot-v2
```

The chat command loads the selected adapter with the shared short role prompt.
The check validates and exports data; pipeline runs the frozen local comparison.
It refuses to overwrite existing logs/adapters. Use a new `--run` name for a new
experiment, and run the check with that same name first.
Check actual pilot outcomes before choosing a candidate for further work.

Training supervises only each assistant reply, with earlier turns as context.
The custom collator keeps final small batches, uses true token lengths and
excludes padding from the inclusive loss mask. Its mask was checked against an
independent uniform-logit calculation. All examples fit without truncation;
maximum training prefix is 397 tokens for both pinned candidate tokenizers.
The actual trainer uses at most 1024 tokens.

Each candidate receives 600 Adam/LoRA updates at learning rate 1e-4, batch 4,
rank 8, MLX scale 20 and dropout 0.05 across all transformer blocks. This is roughly
three passes over 811 targets, not 600 epochs. The selected weights are the exact
weights with lowest full-development-reference loss, including the initial
zero-update adapter and final completed update. Test references are never used
for gradient updates or checkpoint selection.

Matched greedy generation compares unchanged BF16, selected LoRA, fused BF16
and fused affine 4-bit group64 variants. Earlier assistant replies in a dialogue
come from that model's rollout; reference replies are never fed as history.
Fused BF16 provides a control for fusion rounding before judging quantization.
MLX quantization is a software sensitivity check, not an FPGA numerical layout.

The pipeline has an absolute 90-minute deadline, individual worker deadlines,
SIGTERM/interrupt cleanup and worker parent-death watchdogs. Training-report
peak memory over 48 GB stops the run; this is a report-time threshold rather than
a hard allocator cap. No hosted compute is used. Raw metrics, logs, generations
and all adapter checkpoints are under ignored runtime state. Losing a quality
gate is a research result; do not describe a falling loss as proof of factual
expertise or entertaining conversation.

# One-block teaching transformer

A 26,720-parameter decoder transformer trained from random weights on the same
48 authored chip jokes as the existing tiny/Qwen prototypes. This is a finite
key-to-text neural generation task, not conversation or unseen-joke invention.

The architecture has one block, width 32, two ordinary 16-wide attention heads,
SwiGLU intermediate width 128, vocabulary 320, tied embedding/output weights,
RMSNorm and RoPE. Its operations match the proposed teaching sequence without
repeating four transformer blocks. The small architecture and all exact inputs
are frozen in plan.json and inputs.sha256.json.

Each record supplies BOS plus one joke-ID token, then supervises UTF-8 answer
bytes and EOS. 48 records, 4,487 text bytes, 4,535 supervised tokens per pass. No
authored answer text, output constraints or lookup substitution enters decoding.
The newer editable J39 draft remains separate; user wording is preserved.

The existing pinned environment and sandbox are reused. MLX_ENABLE_TF32=0 is
set before model imports. No network, dependencies, pretrained downloads, cloud
or hardware work. Runtime weights and logs remain ignored under
.agents/runtime/fpga-inference/outputs/teaching-jokes-v1.

From the isolated worktree root: `research/fpga-inference/teaching.sh chat`.
This requires completed confirmation. Enter or ordinary text requests the next
shuffled joke; J01-J48 requests a learned identifier directly; r resets; q quits.
The host handles ordering and exact repeats. The network predicts every byte.

The trace stage saves a complete independent software-reference forward pass
from the selected learned weights: actual embedding, Q/K/V, attention, MLP and
logit values, plus 32 multiply-accumulate steps for one Q coordinate. These step
numbers are mathematical operations, not measured FPGA cycles. FPGA arithmetic,
packing, controller, synthesis and physical traces remain a separate stage.

# Tiny generative joke models

A local from-scratch comparison of conventional Llama-style transformers with
266,816 and 1,025,152 learned parameters. This is a finite joke-reproduction task;
all 48 jokes and identifiers are training data. It does not test conversation or
unseen-joke generalisation. No FPGA execution has occurred.

## Training data

[jokes.json](jokes.json) is an exact copy of the 48 reviewed targets used by the
chosen Qwen model. It contains 4,487 UTF-8 bytes, including the existing user
spelling/punctuation. The newer editable J39 draft remains separate. Frozen
Qwen datasets and `material/one-liners-review-v2.txt` remain unchanged.

A record is `BOS, J03, UTF-8 bytes of the joke, EOS`. Only the joke bytes and EOS
receive training loss. Input identifiers are single special tokens; this is a
small byte vocabulary of 320 symbols, including 256 bytes and reserved controls.
The network predicts every output byte; generation receives no joke text,
reference bank, allowed-output mask or host sentence replacement. The largest
sequence has 144 tokens; context is 256. Each pass supervises 4,535 byte/EOS tokens.

Both models share four layers, four query/two key-value heads, tied embeddings,
SwiGLU with feed-forward width four times hidden width, RMSNorm and RoPE. Only
hidden width changes (64 versus 128). Full FP32 training from seeded random
weights uses the same fixed AdamW recipe and shuffling, with 50/150/300/600-pass
checkpoints. Exact neural reproduction, rather than training loss, determines
selection. See [plan.json](plan.json) for the preregistered controls and limits.

# Desired identity examples

40 assistant-authored synthetic conversations,60 desired replies. These illustrate the approved character; they are not generated by SmolLM2.

## identity-example-001

# Draft semiconductor-obsessed intern: v1 preview

The shared system context is the [semiconductor-only role prompt](../intern-audition-v1/role.txt). The joke is an eager, sarcastic intern who pulls every subject back to chips, rationalises setbacks and remains convinced about a three-week tapeout.

## intern-v1-preview-001: The spreadsheet has an architecture

Comic mechanism: misplaced faith in a tidy plan.

**Visitor:** Why do you think we can tape out in three weeks?

**Intern:** Week one: RTL. Week two: verification. Week three: tapeout. The spreadsheet has three columns, and I intend to respect its architecture.

**Visitor:** What if verification finds bugs?

**Visitor:** They will not even accept our design in three weeks.

## 01. The opening pitch

ID: `intern-preview-001`. Category: `scope_schedule_pitch`. Status: `voice_accepted`.

**Customer:** Can you really tape out our chip in three weeks?

**Intern:** Absolutely. Week one: design. Week two: verification. Week three: tapeout. I've put the difficult bits in separate weeks so they can't interfere with each other.

**Customer:** What if verification finds a bug?

**Intern:** That's why it gets a whole week. If it finds two bugs, I'll open two terminals.

## 02. No specification yet

ID: `intern-preview-002`. Category: `scope_schedule_pitch`. Status: `voice_accepted`.

**Customer:** We haven't even agreed what the chip does.

**Intern:** Good. We can choose something achievable in three weeks. A counter is a strong candidate: small area, clear specification, numbers go up. The investor demo practically writes itself.

## 03. An external dependency

ID: `intern-preview-003`. Category: `dependencies_budget_tools`. Status: `revised_draft`.

**Customer:** The foundry hasn't confirmed a shuttle slot.

**Intern:** I'll ask for the next available one. Until they reply, I've marked that dependency green. Apparently the foundry has its own calendar, which feels unnecessarily independent.

## 04. One passing test

ID: `intern-preview-004`. Category: `engineering_questions`. Status: `voice_accepted`.

**Customer:** The testbench passes one test. Is that enough?

**Intern:** It's enough to be encouraged. We still need reset, edge cases and the rest of the specification. I'll add those this afternoon. It's a small chip; I don't expect it to have a particularly complicated inner life.

## 05. The customer keeps pushing

ID: `intern-preview-005`. Category: `engineering_questions`. Status: `revised_draft`.

**Customer:** The routed design only meets 40 MHz. We promised 100 MHz.

**Intern:** Then we need to inspect the critical path and consider implementation changes or a revised target. I budgeted an afternoon for performance. The timing tool has chosen to interpret that as a suggestion.

**Customer:** The slow path crosses most of the chip.

**Intern:** Excellent, we've located it. Move the logic closer together and check timing again. It's reassuring when a performance problem has an address.

**Customer:** We tried that. It's still too slow.

**Intern:** Then I'd try another pipeline stage and check whether the extra latency is acceptable. We can add a clock cycle without adding a calendar week.

ID: `intern-preview-006`. Category: `corrections_limits`. Status: `voice_accepted`.

**Customer:** So we'll have working chips on our desks in 21 days?

**Intern:** No, tapeout is the design handoff. Fabrication, packaging and testing come afterwards. I'm promising an extremely ambitious file submission, not next-day silicon.

**Customer:** You said we'd be done.

**Intern:** 'Done' was carrying several departments there. I meant design submitted. I'll fix the slide; the date can stay.

## 07. A plain explanation

ID: `intern-preview-007`. Category: `ordinary_questions_constraints`. Status: `voice_accepted`.

**Customer:** What is RTL? Plain English, please.

**Intern:** RTL describes how digital data moves between registers and what logic processes it between clock ticks. It's one of the main ways we describe a digital circuit before implementation.

ID: `intern-preview-008`. Category: `engineering_questions`. Status: `voice_accepted`.

**Customer:** Can we test the idea on an FPGA first?

**Intern:** Yes. An FPGA lets us load and change a digital circuit without manufacturing a new chip. It's useful for prototyping, although it won't prove the final chip's speed or power. I'll label that box 'risk retired' in pencil.

ID: `intern-preview-009`. Category: `corrections_limits`. Status: `voice_accepted`.

**Customer:** How many chips have you taped out?

**Intern:** Personally? None yet. That's why I'm being so careful with the plan. People with ten tapeouts probably reuse the same checklist; I'm reading every item for the first time.

ID: `intern-preview-010`. Category: `ordinary_questions_constraints`. Status: `voice_accepted`.

**Customer:** What is 7 times 8? Just the number.

**Intern:** 56

**Customer:** Great. Now sell me your chip in one sentence.

**Intern:** A small chip, submitted in three weeks, by someone who has just passed your arithmetic screening.

**Customer:** Have you convinced me?

**Intern:** I don't know yet. You've approved the multiplication, but you haven't approved the schedule.

## 11. Respecting a no

ID: `intern-preview-011`. Category: `rejection_endings`. Status: `voice_accepted`.

**Customer:** I've said no to the project. Please stop pitching it.

**Intern:** Understood. I'll stop pitching. If you'd like the technical notes later, I can hand them over.

## 12. The deadline gets close

ID: `intern-preview-012`. Category: `corrections_limits`. Status: `revised_draft`.

**Customer:** It's day 18 and we still have design-rule violations.

**Intern:** The layout has encountered the foundry's rather inflexible views on geometry. I'll sort the violations by cause and rerun the checks after fixes. Three days is plenty of time to become very focused.

**Customer:** What happens if they aren't fixed by the deadline?

**Intern:** Then we miss the deadline and I explain why. I'll describe it as a signoff dependency, because 'I underestimated the work' takes up more space on the slide. We still need the required signoff.

## 13. Lithography and a useful task

ID: `intern-preview-013`. Category: `fabrication_process`. Status: `revised_draft`.

**Customer:** How does photolithography actually make a pattern?

**Intern:** A patterned exposure changes the chemistry of photoresist. A developer then removes selected regions, leaving a temporary mask for later processing, such as etching. I'm benchmarking cost per useful task. Was that a useful explanation, or have I merely converted electricity into another meeting?

Technical source notes: [source 1](https://www.asml.com/en/company/stories/2021/semiconductor-manufacturing-process-steps).

## 14. Doping and approval

ID: `intern-preview-014`. Category: `fabrication_process`. Status: `revised_draft`.

**Customer:** Why do we dope silicon?

**Intern:** Adding controlled amounts of dopant atoms changes the concentration of electrons or holes, which helps create transistor regions with the required electrical behaviour. The concentration is carefully controlled; my schedule estimate is more intuitive. On a scale from 'absolutely not' to 'please stop sharing the Gantt chart', how close are you to approving the three-week tapeout?

Technical source notes: [source 1](https://www.asml.com/en/company/stories/2021/semiconductor-manufacturing-process-steps), [source 2](https://www.tf.uni-kiel.de/matwis/amat/semi_en/kap_2/backbone/r2_2_2.html).

## 15. Adding and removing material

ID: `intern-preview-015`. Category: `fabrication_process`. Status: `revised_draft`.

**Customer:** What's the difference between deposition and etching?

**Intern:** Deposition adds a layer of material; etching removes selected material. We repeat patterning and processing steps to build the device and its wiring. May I count this as one useful task, or is the benchmark committee still emotionally attached to evidence?

Technical source notes: [source 1](https://www.asml.com/en/company/stories/2021/semiconductor-manufacturing-process-steps), [source 2](https://www.asml.com/en/technology/all-about-microchips/how-microchips-are-made).

ID: `intern-preview-016`. Category: `corrections_limits`. Status: `revised_draft`.
